<!-- definition-1: body_md -->
An \emph{admissible weight} is an infinite increasing sequence $\mu^{|\infty}=(\mu_j)_{j \ge 1}$ of elements in $\mathbb{R}_{>0}$, i.e.,
    $0< \mu_1 \le \mu_2 \le \cdots$.
<!-- end definition-1 -->
<!-- definition-2: body_md -->
An admissible weight $\mu^{|\infty} = (\mu_j)_{j \ge 1}$ is called \emph{quasianalytic} if 
    \begin{equation} \label{eq:qa}
    \sum_{j \ge 1}  \frac{1}{\mu_j} = \infty.
\end{equation}
<!-- end definition-2 -->
<!-- definition-3: body_md -->
Let $\mu^{|\infty} = (\mu_j)_{j\ge 1}$ be an admissible weight and $M_0>0$.
    Let $N \in \mathbb{N}_{\ge 1} \cup \{\infty\}$.
    A function $f : I \to \mathbb{R}$, defined on a compact interval $I \subseteq \mathbb{R}$,
    is called \emph{$(\mu^{|N},M_0)$-smooth} if $f$ is of class $\mathcal{C}^{N}$ 
    and 
    \begin{equation}
        \|f^{(j)}\|_{I} \le M_j, \quad 0 \le j < N +1.
    \end{equation}
<!-- end definition-3 -->
<!-- definition-4: body_md -->
\label[d]{d:nn}
    Let $\mu^{|\infty}= (\mu_j)_{j\ge 1}$ be an admissible weight and $M_0,a,b>0$.
    We say that $(\mu^{|\infty},M_0,a,b)$ is \emph{admissible}, if 
    \begin{equation} \label{eq:condition}
        \sum_{j=j_0+1}^\infty \frac{1}{\mu_j} > a\, e, \quad \text{ where }  j_0 = \lceil \log (\tfrac{M_0}{b})\rceil_{\mathbb{N}}.
    \end{equation}
    In that case, we define the integer
    \begin{equation} \label{eq:nn}
        \mathbf{N}= \mathbf{N}(\mu^{|\infty},M_0,a,b):= 2\, \sup\Big\{n \in \mathbb{N} : \sum_{j=j_0+1}^n \frac{1}{\mu_j} < a\, e\Big\}
    \end{equation}
    and say that $\mathbf{N}$ is the \emph{degree associated with $(\mu^{|\infty},M_0,a,b)$}.
<!-- end definition-4 -->
<!-- remark-1: body_md -->
\label[r]{r:nnprop}
    (1) By definition, for $r,s>0$, $(r\, \mu^{|\infty},s\, M_0,a,b)$ is admissible if and only 
    if $(\mu^{|\infty},M_0,r\, a, \frac{b}{s})$ is admissible,
    and
    \[
        \mathbf{N}(r \, \mu^{|\infty},s\, M_0,a,b) = \mathbf{N}(\mu^{|\infty},M_0,r\, a, \tfrac{b}{s}).
    \]

    (2) Assuming admissibility, the integer $\mathbf{N}(\mu^{|\infty},M_0,a,b)$ is increasing in $a$ and decreasing in $b$.
<!-- end remark-1 -->
<!-- theorem-1: body_md -->
\label[t]{t:Bezout1} 
    Let $\mu^{|\infty} = (\mu_j)_{j\ge 1}$ be an admissible weight satisfying \eqref{eq:ai} with constant $H\ge 1$. 
    Let $M_0>0$, $B_0\ge b_0 > 0$, and $d \in \mathbb{N}_{\ge 1}$.
    Assume that $(\mu^{|\infty},\tfrac{1}{2} e^{4H\overline m}\, d^{2d} B_0,2,b_0)$ is admissible and let 
    \[ 
        \mathbf{N} = \mathbf{N}(\mu^{|\infty},\tfrac{1}{2} e^{4H\overline m} d^{2d} B_0,2,b_0).
    \]
Let $f : [0,1] \to [0,1]$ be $(\mu^{|\mathbf{N}},M_0)$-smooth 
and  
$p \in \mathcal{P}_2^d$ satisfy $\|p\|_{\Gamma(f)} \ge b_0$ and $\|p\|_{[0,1]^2} \le B_0$.
Then 
\begin{equation}
    \mathbf{z}(p,f)\le \mathbf{N},
\end{equation}
where $\mathbf{z}(p,f)$ denotes the total number of zeros of $p(x,f(x))$, for $x \in [0,1]$, counted with multiplicities.
<!-- end theorem-1 -->
<!-- proposition-1: body_md -->
\label[p]{p:zeros}
   Let $I \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ be a compact interval.
   Let $\mu^{|\infty} = (\mu_j)_{j \ge 1}$ be an admissible weight and $M_0>b_0>0$.
   Assume that $(\mu^{|\infty},M_0,|I|,b_0)$ is admissible and let 
    \[ 
        \mathbf{N} = \mathbf{N}(\mu^{|\infty},M_0,|I|,b_0).
    \]
   Let $f : I \to \mathbb{R}$ be a $(\mu^{|\mathbf{N}}, M_0)$-smooth function satisfying $\|f\|_I \ge b_0$.
   Then the total number of zeros of $f$ in $I$ (counted with multiplicities) is finite and 
   bounded by $\mathbf{N}$.
<!-- end proposition-1 -->
<!-- proposition-2: body_md -->
\label[p]{p:composition}
    Let $\mu^{|\infty} = (\mu_j)_{j\ge 1}$ be an admissible weight satisfying \eqref{eq:ai} with constant $H\ge 1$. 
    Let $M_0>0$.
    If $f : [0,1] \to [0,1]$ is $(\mu^{|N},M_0)$-smooth and $p \in \mathcal{P}_2^d$, 
    then $h := p \circ \overline f : [0,1] \to \mathbb{R}$, where $\overline f : [0,1] \to [0,1]^2$, $\overline f(x) = (x,f(x))$, 
    is $(2\, \mu^{|N}, \tfrac{1}{2} e^{4H\overline m}\,  d^{2d}\, \|p\|_{[0,1]^2})$-smooth.
<!-- end proposition-2 -->
<!-- lemma-1: body_md -->
\label[l]{l:rai}
    Let $\mu^{|\infty} = (\mu_j)_{j\ge 1}$ be an admissible weight satisfying \eqref{eq:ai} with constant $H\ge 1$. 
     Then the sequence $b_j :=a_j^j$ satisfies  
    \begin{equation}
        b_{j_1}b_{j_2} \cdots b_{j_\ell} \le H^\ell \, b_k 
    \end{equation}
    whenever $j_1 + \cdots + j_\ell = k$ and $j_i \ge 1$ for all $1 \le i \le \ell$.
<!-- end lemma-1 -->
<!-- proof-1: body_md -->
By \eqref{eq:ai}, we have $b_i \le H \, b_{j}^{i/j}$ if $i\le j$. 
    Thus, if $j_1 + \cdots + j_\ell = k$ and $j_i \ge 1$ for all $1 \le i \le \ell$, then 
    \begin{equation}
        b_{j_1}b_{j_2} \cdots b_{j_\ell} \le H\, b_k^{j_1/k}\, H\, b_k^{j_2/k} \cdots H\, b_k^{j_\ell/k} 
        = H^\ell \, b_k 
    \end{equation}
    as claimed.
<!-- end proof-1 -->
<!-- lemma-2: body_md -->
\label[l]{l:Markov}
    For all $p \in \mathcal{P}_n^d$ and $j \in \mathbb{N}$,
    \begin{equation}
        \sup_{x \in [0,1]^n}\|d^j p(x)\|_{L^j(\mathbb{R}^n,\mathbb{R})} \le (2nd^2)^j \|p\|_{[0,1]^n}.
    \end{equation}
<!-- end lemma-2 -->
<!-- proof-2: body_md -->
Markov's inequality implies 
\begin{equation}
    \|\partial^\alpha p\|_{[0,1]^n} \le (2d^2)^{|\alpha|}\, \|p\|_{[0,1]^n},
\end{equation}
for all $\alpha \in \mathbb{N}^n$.
Then, for $v^i= (v^i_1,\ldots,v^i_n) \in \mathbb{R}^n$ with $|v^i|\le 1$ and $x \in [0,1]^n$, 
\begin{align*}
    |(d^jp)(x)(v^1,\ldots,v^j)| &= \Big|\sum_{i_1=1, \ldots,i_j=1}^n  \partial_{i_1}\cdots\partial_{i_j} p(x) \, v^1_{i_1}\cdots v^j_{i_j}\Big| 
                                \le (2nd^2)^{j}\, \|p\|_{[0,1]^n}.
\end{align*}
The lemma is proved.
<!-- end proof-2 -->
<!-- proposition-3: body_md -->
\label[p]{p:FdBop}
    Let $f : U \to V$ and $g : V \to W$ be $\mathcal{C}^k$ maps, where $U,V,W$ are open subsets of normed spaces.
    Then, for $x \in U$,
    \begin{equation}
        \frac{d^k(g \circ f)(x)}{k!} = \operatorname{sym} \,\sum  \frac{d^jg(f(x))}{j_1!\cdots j_k!}  \Big( \frac{d^1 f(x)}{1!}\Big)^{j_1}   \cdots \Big( \frac{d^k f(x)}{k!}\Big)^{j_k},
    \end{equation}
    where $j = j_1+ \cdots+j_k$, the sum is taken over all $j_1,\ldots,j_k$ such that 
    $j_1 + 2j_2 + \cdots + kj_k = k$, and
    $\operatorname{sym}$ denotes symmetrization of a multilinear operator.
<!-- end proposition-3 -->
<!-- proposition-4: body_md -->
\label[p]{p:composition2}
    In the setting of \Cref{p:composition},
    the composite
    $h = p \circ \overline f : [0,1] \to \mathbb{R}$
    is $(2\, \mu^{|N}, \tfrac{1}{2}  (4 d^2 H \hat m)^d\, \|p\|_{[0,1]^2})$-smooth, where
    \begin{equation} \label{eq:olm2}
        \hat m := \max \Big\{  M_0\sqrt{1+\tfrac{1}{M_1^2}},1\Big\}.
    \end{equation}
<!-- end proposition-4 -->
<!-- proof-3: body_md -->
It suffices to modify the estimate \eqref{eq:est} in the following way:
    \begin{align*}
        \frac{|h^{(k)}(x)|}{k!} 
    &\le \|p\|_{[0,1]^2} \, b_k\,  \sum_{j \le d}  \frac{(4\, d^2 H \hat m)^j}{j_1!\cdots j_k!}
\le (4\, d^2 H \hat m)^d\, \|p\|_{[0,1]^2} \, b_k\,  \sum  \frac{j! }{j_1!\cdots j_k!}.
   \end{align*}
   Then the proof of \Cref{p:composition} implies the statement.
<!-- end proof-3 -->
<!-- remark-2: body_md -->
An example, where $d$ is small, is the number of fixed points of $f$.  
    Indeed, the polynomial $p(X,Y) = X-Y$ satisfies $\|p\|_{[0,1]^2} = 1$ and $\deg p =1$.
    Assume that $(\mu^{|\infty},M_0(1+\frac{1}{M_1}),1,b_0)$ is admissible and let 
    \[ 
        \mathbf{N} = \mathbf{N}(\mu^{|\infty}, M_0(1+\tfrac{1}{M_1}) ,1,b_0).
    \]
    Let $f : [0,1] \to [0,1]$ be $(\mu^{|\mathbf{N}},M_0)$-smooth with $\sup_{x\in [0,1]} |x-f(x)|\ge b_0$. 
    By a direct computation,
    the composite function $h(x) = p(x,f(x)) = x-f(x)$, $x \in [0,1]$, is 
    $(\mu^{|\mathbf{N}}, M_0(1+\tfrac{1}{M_1}))$-smooth. (Alternatively, one can use \Cref{p:composition2} which 
    however gives weaker bounds in this case.)
    Moreover, $\|h\|_{[0,1]}\ge b_0$. 
    By \Cref{p:zeros}, the total number of fixed points of $f$ (counted with multiplicities) 
is finite and bounded by $\mathbf{N}$.
<!-- end remark-2 -->
<!-- definition-5: body_md -->
Let $\mathcal{V} \subseteq C^0([0,1]^n,\mathbb{R})$ be a finite dimensional subspace.
    A compact subset $Z \subseteq [0,1]^n$ is said to be \emph{$\mathcal{V}$-norming} if there is a constant $C>0$ 
    such that 
    \begin{equation}
        \|v\|_{[0,1]^n} \le C \, \|v\|_Z, \quad v \in \mathcal{V}.
    \end{equation}
    The infimum of all such constants $C$ is denoted by $N_{\mathcal{V}}(Z)$ and called the \emph{$\mathcal{V}$-norming constant of $Z$}.
This is an inequality of Remez type on a set of zero measure.
<!-- end definition-5 -->
<!-- theorem-2: body_md -->
\label[t]{c:zded}
    Let $\mu^{|\infty} = (\mu_j)_{j\ge 1}$ be an admissible quasianalytic weight satisfying \eqref{eq:ai} with constant $H\ge1$. 
    Let $M_0>0$.
If $f : [0,1] \to [0,1]$ is a transcendental $(\mu^{|\infty},M_0)$-smooth function, 
then, for each $p \in \mathcal{P}_2^d\setminus \{0\}$, 
\begin{equation} \label{eq:zep}
    \mathbf{z}(p,f) \le \eta_{\mu^{|\infty}}\big( 2d \log d + \mathbf{e}(p,f) + 4H \overline m -\log 2 \big).
\end{equation}
Consequently,
\begin{equation} \label{eq:ze}
    \mathbf{z}_d(f) \le  \eta_{\mu^{|\infty}} \big( 2d \log d + \mathbf{e}_d(f) + 4H \overline m -\log 2 \big), \quad d \ge 1.
\end{equation}
<!-- end theorem-2 -->
<!-- proof-4: body_md -->
By (the proof of) \Cref{t:Bezout1},
    \begin{equation} 
        \mathbf{z}(p,f) \le \mathbf{N}(\mu^{|\infty},\tfrac{1}{2} e^{4 H \overline m} d^{2d}\,\|p\|_{[0,1]^2},2,\|p\|_{\Gamma(f)}).
    \end{equation}
    Now, by the properties of $\mathbf{N}$ (see \Cref{r:nnprop}),
    \begin{align}
        \mathbf{N}(\mu^{|\infty},\tfrac{1}{2} e^{4 H \overline m} d^{2d}\,\|p\|_{[0,1]^2},2,\|p\|_{\Gamma(f)}) 
        &=  
        \mathbf{N}\Big(\mu^{|\infty},\tfrac{1}{2} e^{4 H \overline m} d^{2d}\,\frac{\|p\|_{[0,1]^2}}{\|p\|_{\Gamma(f)}},2,1\Big)
        \\
        &=
        \eta_{\mu^{|\infty}}\big(2d \log d + \mathbf{e}(p,f) + 4H \overline m -\log 2\big)
    \end{align}
    implying \eqref{eq:zep}.
    Since $\eta_{\mu^{|\infty}}$ is increasing, \eqref{eq:ze} is immediate from \eqref{eq:zep}.
<!-- end proof-4 -->
<!-- corollary-1: body_md -->
Let $f : [0,1] \to [0,1]$ be real analytic and transcendental. 
There exist $C,\rho>0$ (depending on $f$) such that 
\begin{equation} \label{eq:an1}
    \mathbf{z}_d(f) \le 2\, e^{2e\rho+1} \Big(2d\log d + \mathbf{e}_d(f)  + 4 C\sqrt{1 + \tfrac{1}{C^2\rho^2}} +1 -\log 2\Big), \quad d\ge 1.
\end{equation}
<!-- end corollary-1 -->
<!-- proof-5: body_md -->
In this case, $H=1$, $M_0 = C$, and $M_1 = C\rho$. 
    The bound follows from \eqref{eq:ze} and \eqref{eq:an}.
<!-- end proof-5 -->
<!-- corollary-2: body_md -->
\label[c]{c:en}
Let $f : [0,1] \to [0,1]$ be transcendental and the restriction of an entire function. 
There exists $C=C(f)>0$ such that 
\begin{equation}
    \mathbf{z}_d(f) \le 12\,d\log d + 6\, \mathbf{e}_d(f)  + C, \quad d\ge 1.
\end{equation}
<!-- end corollary-2 -->
<!-- proof-6: body_md -->
Choose $\tau>0$ such that $2e\tau +1 \le \log 3$ and apply \eqref{eq:an1} for $\rho = \tau$.
<!-- end proof-6 -->
<!-- theorem-3: body_md -->
\label[t]{t:BY}
    Let $f$ be a non-polynomial entire function on $\mathbb{C}^n$ that is real on $\mathbb{R}^n$.
    Assume that the graph $\Gamma(f|_{\mathbb{R}^n})$ of $f|_{\mathbb{R}^n}$ 
    intersects $[0,1]^{n+1}$ 
    in a subset $Z$ of real dimension $n$.
    Then there exists a sequence of positive integers $d_j \to \infty$ and a sequence of positive reals $\epsilon_j \to 0$ 
    such that 
    \begin{equation}
    \log N_{\mathcal{P}_{n+1}^{d_j}}(Z) \le d_j^{2+\epsilon_j},\quad  \text{ for all } j.
    \end{equation}
    The sequence $(d_j)$ depends only on $f$ and the sequence $(\epsilon_j)$ only on $f$, $n$, and the $n$-dimensional Hausdorff measure of $Z$.
<!-- end theorem-3 -->
<!-- corollary-3: body_md -->
Let $f : [0,1] \to [0,1]$ be transcendental and the restriction of an entire function that is real on $\mathbb{R}$. 
There exists a sequence of positive integers $d_j \to \infty$, a sequence of positive reals $\epsilon_j \to 0$, 
and a constant
$C>0$ such that 
\begin{equation}
    \mathbf{z}_{d_j}(f) \le 6\, d_j^{2+ \epsilon_j} + 12\, d_j \log d_j + C, \quad  \text{ for all } j.
\end{equation}
<!-- end corollary-3 -->
<!-- proof-7: body_md -->
Combine \Cref{c:en} with \Cref{t:BY}.
<!-- end proof-7 -->
<!-- remark-3: body_md -->
\label[r]{r:sp}
For each $\zeta \in (0,1)$,
    there exists an analytic function $f$ defined in a neighborhood of $[0,1]$ 
    and a sequence of positive integers $d_j \to \infty$ satisfying 
    \[
        \mathbf{z}_{d_j}(f) \ge e^{d_j^\zeta}, \quad \text{ for all } j.
    \]
    See \cite[Remark 5.3]{Comte:2018aa}. 
    In view of \eqref{eq:an1}, we conclude that 
    \begin{equation} 
        \mathbf{e}_{d_j}(f) \ge c_1\, e^{d_j^\zeta} - 2 d_j \log d_j  - C_2, \quad \text{ for all } j,
    \end{equation}
    for constants $c_1 = c_1(f) \in (0,1)$ and $C_2 = C_2(f) >0$.
<!-- end remark-3 -->
<!-- definition-6: body_md -->
\label[d]{d:Dw}
Let $s\in [0,\infty)$ and set $k = \lceil s\rceil \in \mathbb{N}$ and $\sigma = k-s \in [0,1)$.  
We define 
\begin{equation}
    (\mu_s)_j := j L_1(e_kj) L_2(e_k j) \cdots L_{k-1}(e_k j) (L_k(e_k j))^{1-\sigma}, \quad  j\ge 1.
\end{equation}
Then $\mu_s^{|\infty} := ((\mu_s)_j)_{j \ge 1}$ is an admissible quasianalytic weight for all $s \in [0,\infty)$. 
(Quasianalyticity follows from the integral test, in view of \eqref{eq:it}.)
Since $(\mu_s)_j/j$ is increasing, so is the sequence $a_j$ defined in \eqref{eq:aj}, i.e., \eqref{eq:ai} holds with $H=1$. 

The sequences $\mu_s^{|\infty}$ are called \emph{Denjoy weights}.
Note that $\mu_0^{|\infty}$ coincides with the analytic weight $\mu_{\operatorname{an}}^{|\infty}$.
<!-- end definition-6 -->
<!-- proposition-5: body_md -->
\label[p]{p:Denjoy}
    Let $s \ge 0$ and $a\ge 1$. Then $\eta_{a\,\mu_s^{|\infty}} : \mathbb{N}_{\ge 1} \to \mathbb{N}$ is bounded by a polynomial  if and only if $s \in [0,1]$.  
    
    For $s=k \in \mathbb{N}$ and $m \in \mathbb{N}_{\ge 1}$, 
    \begin{equation} \label{eq:k} 
        \frac{E_{k+1}(f_k(a,m)-1)}{e_k}-1   \le  \tfrac{1}{2}\eta_{a\, \mu_{k}^{|\infty}}(m)  \le \frac{E_{k+1}(f_k(a,m)+1)}{e_k}-1,
\end{equation}
where $f_k(a,m) := 2a e+ L_{k+1}(e_k(m+1))$.
In particular,
\begin{align} \label{eq:k0}
    e^{2ae-1}(m+1)-1 \le &\tfrac{1}{2}\eta_{a\, \mu_{0}^{|\infty}}(m) \le e^{2ae+1} (m+1) - 1,
    \\ \label{eq:k1}
  e^{e^{2ae  -1}-1} (m+1)^{e^{2ae -1}}-1  \le &\tfrac{1}{2}\eta_{a\, \mu_{1}^{|\infty}}(m) \le e^{e^{2ae  +1}-1} (m+1)^{e^{2ae  +1}}-1.
\end{align}
<!-- end proposition-5 -->
<!-- proof-8: body_md -->
Let us first prove \eqref{eq:k}.
Set
$A^k_n := \sum_{j=1}^n \frac{1}{(\mu_k)_j}$, for $n \ge 1$, and $A^k_0 := 0$.
    Consider $g(t) = L_{k+1}(e_k t)$, for $t \ge 1$. Then
    \begin{align} \label{eq:it}
        g'(t) &= \frac{1}{t L_1(e_kt) L_2(e_k t) \cdots L_k(e_k t)}
    \end{align}
    is decreasing, i.e., $g$ is concave. Thus
    \[
        g(j+1) - g(j) \le g'(j) \le g(j) - g(j-1), 
    \]
    where the left inequality holds for $j\ge 1$ and the right for $j \ge 2$.
    Summing over $j$, we find 
    \[
        g(n+1) - g(1) \le A^k_n \quad \text{ and } \quad A^k_n -A^k_1 \le g(n)-g(1)   
    \]
    which implies 
    \begin{equation} \label{eq:A1}
        L_{k+1}(e_k(n+1)) \le  A^k_n 
    \le L_{k+1}(e_k n) + 1, \quad n \ge 1.
    \end{equation}

    For $x > 1$ define the positive integer $n(x)$ by 
    \begin{equation} \label{eq:A1x}
        A^k_{n(x)} < x \le A^k_{n(x)+1}.
    \end{equation}
    By \eqref{eq:A1} and \eqref{eq:A1x},
    \begin{equation} \label{eq:A1n}
        \frac{E_{k+1}(x-1)}{e_k}- 1  \le  n(x) < \frac{E_{k+1}(x)}{e_k}- 1.
    \end{equation}



    By \eqref{eq:A1x}, we have 
    \begin{equation}
        \sum_{j=m+1}^{n(x)} \frac{1}{(\mu_k)_j}  < x- A^k_{m} \le  \sum_{j=m+1}^{n(x)+1} \frac{1}{(\mu_k)_j}
    \end{equation}
    so that, setting $x = 2ae +A^k_{m}$, we get 
    \[
         \sum_{j=m+1}^{n} \frac{1}{(\mu_k)_j} < 2ae \le \sum_{j=m+1}^{n+1} \frac{1}{(\mu_k)_j} 
    \]
    with $n=n(2ae + A^k_{m})$, since $2ae+ A^k_{m}> 1$.
    Thus, by \eqref{eq:A1} and \eqref{eq:A1n},
    \begin{equation}
        \frac{E_{k+1}(2ae-1 +L_{k+1}(e_k (m+1)))}{e_k}-1  \le n \le \frac{E_{k+1}(2ae+1 +L_{k+1}(e_k (m+1)))}{e_k}-1.
    \end{equation}
    This implies \eqref{eq:k}, since $n=\frac{1}{2} \eta_{a\,\mu_k^{|\infty}}(m)$. 

    Now \eqref{eq:k0} and \eqref{eq:k1} easily follow from \eqref{eq:k}.
    Since $(\mu_{s})_j \le (\mu_{t})_j$ for all $j$ if $s \le t$ and thus $\eta_{a\, \mu_{s}^{|\infty}} \le \eta_{a\, \mu_{t}^{|\infty}}$, 
    we conclude that  $\eta_{a\, \mu_{s}^{|\infty}}$ 
    is bounded by a polynomial, for all $s\in [0,1]$.

To see that $\eta_{a\, \mu_{s}^{|\infty}}$  cannot be bounded by a polynomial if $s>1$ it is enough to show this for $s \in (1,2)$
and $a=1$.
Fix such $s$, let $\sigma = 2 -s \in (0,1)$, and
    consider $g(t) = (\log\log(e^e t))^{\sigma}$, for $t\ge 1$. Since 
    \[
        g'(t) = \frac{\sigma}{t \log(e^e t) (\log\log(e^et))^{1-\sigma}}
    \]
    and $g$ is concave, we find similarly to \eqref{eq:A1},
    \begin{equation} \label{eq:ll1}
        (\log \log(e^e (n+1)))^{\sigma} -1  \le  \sigma A^s_n \le (\log \log(e^e n))^{\sigma} - 1 +\tfrac{\sigma}{e}, \quad n\ge 1, 
    \end{equation}
    where $A^s_n = \sum_{j=1}^n \frac{1}{(\mu_s)_j}$ and noting that $A^s_1 = \frac{1}{e}$. As above,
    let $n(x)$, for $x>1$, be the positive integer satisfying $A^s_{n(x)} < x \le A^s_{n(x)+1}$. Then, by \eqref{eq:ll1},
    \begin{equation}
        e_2(n(x)+1) \ge  E_2((\sigma x +1 -\tfrac{\sigma}{e})^{\frac{1}{\sigma}}) 
    \end{equation}
    and, setting $n = n(2e + A^s_m) =\frac{1}{2} \eta_{\mu_{s}^{|\infty}}(m)$, we find
   \begin{align*}
       e_2(n+1) &\ge  E_2((2\sigma e + \sigma A^s_m +1 -\tfrac{\sigma}{e})^{\frac{1}{\sigma}})      
       \ge E_2(((2 e -\tfrac{1}{e})\sigma + (L_2(e_2 (m+1)))^{\sigma} )^{\frac{1}{\sigma}}).
   \end{align*}
   Suppose for contradiction that $n$ can be bounded by a polynomial in $m$. Then there exist $C\ge 1$ and $N \in \mathbb{N}_{\ge 1}$
   such that, for all $m$, 
   \[
       E_2(((2 e -\tfrac{1}{e})\sigma  + (L_2(e_2 (m+1)))^{\sigma} )^{\frac{1}{\sigma}}) \le C (e_2(m+1))^N,
   \]
   or equivalently,
   \begin{equation} \label{eq:con}
       (2 e -\tfrac{1}{e})\sigma    \le  (L_2(C (e_2(m+1))^N))^\sigma - (L_2(e_2 (m+1)))^{\sigma}.
   \end{equation}
   Setting $z=e_2(m+1)$, we have
   \begin{align}
       L_2(C (e_2(m+1))^N)& = L_2(C z^N) = \log(\log C + N \log z) 
       \\
                                       &= \log\Big(N\log z \Big(1+\frac{\log C}{N \log z}\Big) \Big)
       \\
                                       &= \log\log z + \log N + o(1)
   \end{align}
   as $z \to \infty$.
   By the mean value theorem, the right-hand side of \eqref{eq:con} equals
   \begin{align} \label{eq:mvt}
       (\log\log z + \log N + o(1))^\sigma - (\log\log z)^{\sigma} = \sigma \zeta^{\sigma-1} (\log N + o(1)),
   \end{align}
   for some $\zeta$ between $\log\log z + \log N + o(1)$ and $\log\log z$. 
   Since $\sigma \in (0,1)$, \eqref{eq:mvt} tends to zero as $z \to \infty$ which contradicts \eqref{eq:con}.
<!-- end proof-8 -->
<!-- corollary-4: body_md -->
\label[c]{c:Denjoy1}
    Let $s \in [0,1]$. 
    If $f : [0,1] \to [0,1]$ is a transcendental $(\mu_s^{|\infty},M_0)$-smooth function, then
    $\mathbf{z}_d(f)$ is bounded by a polynomial in $d$ and $\mathbf{e}_d(f)$.
<!-- end corollary-4 -->
<!-- proof-9: body_md -->
This is a consequence of \Cref{c:zded} and \Cref{p:Denjoy}.
<!-- end proof-9 -->
<!-- corollary-5: body_md -->
\label[c]{c:rat}
    Let $s \in [0,1]$ and let $f : [0,1] \to [0,1]$ be a transcendental function of class 
    $\mathcal{C}_{M_s}$ associated with the Denjoy weight $\mu_s^{|\infty}$ (with $(M_s)_0=1$)
    such that $\mathbf{e}_d(f)$ is bounded by a polynomial in $d$.
    Then the number of rational points of height at most $H$ on the graph of $f$ is bounded by a polynomial in $\log H$.
<!-- end corollary-5 -->
<!-- proof-10: body_md -->
By \cite[Proposition 2.4]{Pila:2006ab}, the set $\Gamma(f)(\mathbb{Q};H)$ of rational points of height at most $H$ in $\Gamma(f)$ 
is contained in the union of at most $6B (\frac{(d+1)(d+2)}{2})^C\, H^{8/(d+3)}$ algebraic curves of degree $d$, where $d \ge 5$ and $B,C$ 
are constants depending on the class of $f$. (The Denjoy--Carleman class $\mathcal{C}_{M_s}$ is contained in the class $M(B,C)$ 
of mild functions used in \cite{Pila:2006ab}.)

Let $d = \lfloor \log H \rfloor$, assuming that $H \ge e$.
Then $\Gamma(f)(\mathbb{Q};H)$ is contained in the union of at most
\[
    6B\, 3^C\, e^8 (\log H)^{2C}
\]
algebraic curves of degree $d$, using that $\frac{(d+1)(d+2)}{2} \le 3 (\log H)^2$ and $H^{8/(d+3)} \le e^8$.
Thus, the number of points in 
$\Gamma(f)(\mathbb{Q};H)$ is bounded by
\[
    6B\, 3^C\, e^8 (\log H)^{2C} \cdot \mathbf{z}_{\lfloor \log H \rfloor}(f)
\]
which is bounded by a polynomial in $\log H$, by \Cref{c:Denjoy1}, provided that 
$\mathbf{e}_d(f)$ is bounded by a polynomial in $d$. Thus \Cref{c:rat} is proved.
<!-- end proof-10 -->
<!-- definition-7: body_md -->
\label[d]{d:fa}
 Let $\mu^{|\infty} = (\mu_j)_{j \ge 1}$ be any admissible weight (not necessarily quasianalytic) and $M_0=1$ such that 
 the associated function
\[
    \omega_M(t) := \sup_{k \in \mathbb{N}} \log \frac{t^k}{M_k}, \quad t>0,
\]
satisfies $\omega_M(t) = o(t)$ and $\omega_M(2t) = O(\omega_M(t))$ as $t \to \infty$. 
Let $\xi = (\xi_n)_{n \ge 1}$ be a sequence of independent random variables, each uniformly distributed on $[-1,1]$.
    Define
    \begin{equation}
        f_\xi(x) := \tfrac{1}{2} + \sum_{n\ge 1} \xi_n c_n \cos(2\pi n x), \quad \text{ where } c_n := \frac{1}{4 n^2 e^{\omega_M(2\pi n)}}.
    \end{equation}
<!-- end definition-7 -->
<!-- remark-4: body_md -->
Note that $\omega_M(t) = o(t)$ as $t \to \infty$ means that $\mathcal{C}_M$ contains the real analytic functions as 
a proper subclass. This condition is satisfied if the associated sequence $a_j$ (see \eqref{eq:aj}) tends to $\infty$.
Moreover, $\omega_M(2t) = O(\omega_M(t))$ as $t \to \infty$ is a technical condition which holds provided that $\liminf_{j \to \infty} \frac{\mu_{\ell j}}{\mu_j} >1$ for some 
positive integer $\ell$; see \cite[Lemma 12]{BMM07}.
Clearly, these conditions are satisfied by all Denjoy weights.
Moreover, $\log t = o(\omega_M(t))$ as $t \to \infty$ by definition.
<!-- end remark-4 -->
<!-- proposition-6: body_md -->
\label[p]{p:as}
    The family $\{f_\xi\}$ has the following properties:
    \begin{enumerate}
        \item $f_\xi : [0,1] \to [0,1]$ belongs to $\mathcal{C}_M$.
        \item Almost surely, $f_\xi$ is not real analytic. More generally, almost surely $f_\xi$ does not belong to any class $\mathcal{C}_{L}$ with $\omega_M(t) = o(\omega_L(t))$ as $t \to \infty$, 
            where $L$ is any weight sequence as in \Cref{d:fa}.
        \item  Almost surely, $\mathbf{e}_d(f_\xi)$ is bounded by a polynomial in $d$ of degree $7$ (whose coefficients depend on $\xi$). 
    \end{enumerate}
<!-- end proposition-6 -->
<!-- theorem-4: body_md -->
\label{t:rp}
    Let $M = M_s$ a Denjoy weight for $s \in (0,1]$ with $(M_s)_0 =1$. 
    Then, for the family $\{f_\xi\}$,
    the number of rational points of height at most $H$ on the graph of $f_\xi$ is almost surely bounded by a polynomial in $\log H$.
<!-- end theorem-4 -->
<!-- proof-11: body_md -->
This follows from \Cref{c:rat} and \Cref{p:as}. 
    Note that $f_\xi$ is almost surely transcendent, because if there exists a nonzero polynomial $p \in \mathbb{R}[X,Y]$ such that $p(x,f_\xi(x)) = 0$, for all $x \in [0,1]$, 
    then $f_\xi$ is real analytic. 
    Indeed, the $1$-periodic function $f_\xi$ belongs to $\mathcal{C}_{M_s}(\mathbb{R})$ and, by quasianalyticity, $p(x,f_\xi(x))=0$, for all $x \in \mathbb{R}$.
    By \cite[Theorem 2]{Siciak70} or \cite[Proposition VI.3.11]{Malgrange66}, $f_\xi$ is real analytic.
<!-- end proof-11 -->
